instruction: Several cattle in the grazing area are drooling heavily, lame, and have raw sores in the mouth. A buyer says I should move them quickly before the rest of the herd looks sick. What should I do first?
output: Treat this as suspected foot-and-mouth disease or another notifiable disease. Do not move, sell, or take the animals to auction. Keep the affected cattle away from other herds as much as you can and report it urgently to the nearest State Veterinarian or animal-health official. When several cattle at once show drooling, mouth lesions, and lameness, the safest action is reporting and movement restriction, not home treatment.

instruction: If I suspect a disease that must be reported but I cannot reach the state vet immediately, do I have to wait, or can I tell someone else first?
output: Do not wait. A suspected notifiable disease should be reported immediately. If you cannot reach a veterinary official at once, the regulations also allow you to notify a police officer, who must pass the report on without delay. While reporting, isolate the suspect animal and keep other animals and unnecessary people away from it.

instruction: A dog that was snapping and behaving strangely has bitten one of my goats and also tried to bite people at the homestead. Can I just tie it up and wait until tomorrow?
output: Do not treat this casually. A strangely aggressive biting animal must be treated as possible rabies. Notify a veterinary official immediately. The animal must be securely confined so it cannot bite more people or animals, or killed if safe confinement is not possible. Anyone who may have been bitten or had contact with saliva through a wound should seek medical attention at once.

instruction: Do cattle here need anthrax vaccination every year, or only when there is an outbreak? And what if I suspect anthrax anyway?
output: Under the regulations, cattle older than three months should be vaccinated against anthrax once every 12 months with an approved vaccine. Even if animals are vaccinated, any suspected anthrax case still needs to be reported to a veterinary official immediately. Suspected anthrax is not something to manage quietly at home.

instruction: We are in Omusati and want to move cloven-hoofed animals to another place. If there is suspected foot-and-mouth disease around us, can we still move them if we are careful?
output: No. During foot-and-mouth disease risk or control, movement of cloven-hoofed animals, their products, and restricted material must follow the legal movement-control rules. Do not move the animals just because they look quiet or because you plan to be careful. If FMD is suspected, movement should stop and veterinary instructions must be followed immediately.
